quote: Muss es möglich sein zu ent- scheiden über die Quadratur des Kreises?
english: Must it be possible to decide about the squaring of the circle?
topic: Philosophical questions on whether human reason can answer every question it poses itself (decidability, squaring the circle, contradictory results), followed by a Plücker-type formula for the dimension of plane algebraic curves.

triage.modern_statement: Read literally: can it be decided whether a circle can be squared, i.e. whether a square of equal area can be built from a given circle with straightedge and compass? That is the same as asking whether π is a constructible number. The note sits among philosophical questions about whether reason can answer every question it poses, so it is really being used as a test case for a broader question: is every precisely posed mathematical problem decidable, either by a solution or by a proof that no solution exists?
triage.answered_by: The specific question was settled by Ferdinand von Lindemann in 1882. He proved that π is transcendental (the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem), so squaring the circle with straightedge and compass is impossible. Hilbert himself later used this as his standard example of a problem settled by an impossibility proof. He did so in his 1900 Paris lecture 'Mathematical Problems', the preamble to his 23 problems, where he held that every mathematical problem is solvable ('in mathematics there is no ignorabimus'). The general solvability question behind the note was later answered in the negative, in a formal sense, by Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) and by Church and Turing (1936), who showed the Entscheidungsproblem has no solution.

evidence.claim: In 1882 squaring the circle was proven impossible as a consequence of the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem, which shows that π is transcendental.
Ferdinand von Lindemann proved in 1882 that squaring the circle is impossible with classical tools.

In his 1900 ICM lecture, Hilbert listed the squaring of the circle among old problems resolved by proofs that certain solutions are impossible. He used this to support his view that every mathematical problem can be settled.
A historical paper on Hilbert's 'no ignorabimus' explicitly links his solvability conviction to impossibility proofs such as squaring the circle, and to the later decision problem and decidability.
Church and Turing proved in 1936 that a general decision algorithm (Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem) is impossible.
Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems show that every consistent axiomatization of number theory contains undecidable propositions.

triage.why: As a concrete question, squaring the circle has been closed since Lindemann's 1882 proof. It is not one of the 23 problems, but it appears in the 1900 lecture's preamble as Hilbert's key example of a solution 'by impossibility proof'. The broader philosophical question in the note, whether every problem must be decidable, became Hilbert's published 'no ignorabimus' stance. Gödel, Church and Turing then answered it in the negative for formal systems. The notebook page's date isn't confirmed here, so it is unclear whether Hilbert wrote this before or after Lindemann's proof. Undecidability and computability remain active fields, but the question as Hilbert wrote it is no longer open.
